theme: LORD, you were favorable, will you not revive us again?
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 85. You read this psalm in Unit 13 as a prayer for revival in exile. Read it now as the prayer of people who are back in the land and find that the glory is not what they hoped. Notice again verses 10 to 13.
settingTheScene: Psalm 85 begins by recalling that God has been favorable to his land and restored the fortunes of Jacob. For the returned exiles, this meant the decree of Cyrus. But the psalm goes on to ask, “Will you not revive us again?” It fits the period of Ezra and Haggai, when the people had returned and still lacked the full blessing. On Day 430 you read it as a lament from the dark side of exile. Today read it as a post-return prayer.
observation: “LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob” (v. 1).
“You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin” (v. 2).
“Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!” (v. 4).
“Will you be angry with us forever? Will you prolong your anger to all generations?” (v. 5).
“Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” (v. 6).
“Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people” (v. 8).
“Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other” (v. 10).
“Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way” (v. 13).
interpretation:
The post-return period was a time of mixed feelings. The people had been brought home, but life was hard. Crops failed, the economy was poor, the temple lagged, and neighbors were hostile. Haggai said that they earned wages and put them in a bag with holes. It would have been easy to think that God was still angry.

The psalm answers by returning to history: God has already forgiven. “You covered all their sin.” It is a statement of faith that does not depend on present feelings. The past forgiveness is the ground for the present request. “Restore us again.” We are allowed to ask God to do again what he has already done.

The psalmist then does something wise. He stops talking and listens: “Let me hear what God the LORD will speak.” The word is peace, but with a condition: “Let them not turn back to folly.” Peace is for those who fear him, and God’s salvation is near to them. The glory will dwell in the land.

The great picture follows. Steadfast love and faithfulness meet. Righteousness and peace kiss. Faithfulness springs from the ground and righteousness looks down from heaven. The Lord will give what is good. This is a vision of heaven and earth cooperating. For Ezra’s generation, it was a hope: someday the land would be so blessed. For us it points to Christ, in whom heaven and earth meet.

The last line is a promise of a path: righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way. God is coming. His footsteps prepare the road.
connection: Luke 1:78-79 says, “The sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness… to guide our feet into the way of peace.” John 1:14 says the Word became flesh, full of grace and truth. Colossians 1:20 says God made peace by the blood of his cross. Romans 5:1: “Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God.” Ephesians 2:14: “He himself is our peace.” Isaiah 40:3 speaks of preparing the way of the LORD.
application:
Pray “Will you not revive us again?” for your church or community.

Be still and ask what God is speaking. Listen for five minutes.

Thank God that in Christ, steadfast love and faithfulness have met, and righteousness and peace have kissed.
prayerPrompts: Ask him to speak peace to you and keep you from turning back to folly.
Thank him that righteousness and peace will kiss.
